content: A poppy is a type of flowering plant that belongs to the poppy family. These plants are known for their striking and colorful flowers, which typically grow one per stem. Poppies can be found as wildflowers, either growing individually or in large clusters, and many species are also cultivated in gardens. Garden varieties include both large plants suitable for mixed herbaceous borders and smaller plants ideal for rock or alpine gardens. The flowers of poppies come in a wide range of colors, including white, pink, yellow, orange, red, and blue. Some species also feature dark center markings. Cultivated varieties, which have been bred over many years, display an even broader spectrum of colors, from deep, solid hues to soft pastel shades. The structure of a poppy flower includes a central whorl of stamens surrounded by a cupor bowl-shaped arrangement of four to six petals. Before blooming, the petals are crumpled within the bud, and as the flower matures, the petals often flatten out before eventually falling away. Poppies are classified into several genera, including: Meconopsis: Includes the Himalayan poppy and Welsh poppy. Papaver: Includes species such as the Iceland poppy, Oriental poppy, Opium poppy, and corn poppy, along with approximately 120 other species. Romneya: Includes the Matilija poppy. Eschscholzia: Includes the California poppy. Stylophorum: Includes the celandine-poppy, mock poppy, yellow-poppy, and wood-poppy. Argemone: Includes the prickly-poppy. Canbya: Includes the pygmy-poppy. Stylomecon: Includes the wind-poppy. Arctomecon: Includes the desert bearclaw-poppy. Hunnemannia: Includes the tulip poppy. Dendromecon: Includes the tree poppy. The pollen of poppies varies by species. For example, the Oriental poppy (Papaver orientale) produces dark blue pollen, while the field or corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas) has pollen that ranges from dark blue to gray. Bees often use poppies as a source of pollen. The opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) is cultivated for its latex, which is used to produce opium and opiates, as well as for its seeds, which are used in cooking and baking, such as in Hungarian poppy seed rolls. Symbolism of Poppies Poppies have historically symbolized both sleep and death. The association with sleep arises from the opium extracted from the plant, while the connection to death is linked to the blood-red color of many poppy species. In Greco-Roman mythology, poppies were offered to the dead and were often depicted on tombstones to signify eternal sleep. This symbolism was famously used in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, where magical poppy fields caused those who entered them to fall into a deep, eternal sleep. Poppies also symbolize resurrection and hope, as their bright scarlet color was seen as a promise of life after death in Greco-Roman traditions. The red corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas) became a symbol of wartime remembrance, particularly for soldiers who died in World War I. This association arose because the corn poppy was one of the few plants that thrived on the battlefields of Europe, where the soil had been heavily disturbed by shelling. The sight of these red flowers blooming amidst the devastation inspired their use as a symbol of sacrifice and remembrance. In Commonwealth countries, artificial poppies made of paper are worn in the weeks leading up to Remembrance Day on November 11 to honor the sacrifices of veterans and civilians in World War I and other conflicts. The Royal British Legion uses the poppy as part of its Poppy Appeal, while in Canada, the Royal Canadian Legion distributes poppies each fall. The design of the Canadian poppy has evolved over time, with the center color changing from green to black to better reflect the appearance of the French poppy. In New Zealand and Australia, paper poppies are distributed by the Returned Services Association in the lead-up to ANZAC Day on April 25. Additionally, the golden poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is the state flower of California. False Positive Drug Tests Although opium is primarily extracted from the latex of unripe poppy seed pods, all parts of the plant, including the seeds, can contain trace amounts of opium alkaloids such as morphine and codeine. This means that consuming foods containing poppy seeds, such as muffins or bagels, can result in a false positive for opiates on drug tests. This phenomenon was popularized in an episode of Seinfeld and later confirmed by experiments on the television program MythBusters. In one experiment, a participant who consumed a loaf of poppy seed cake tested positive for opiates within 30 minutes, while another participant who ate three poppy seed bagels tested positive two hours later. Both participants continued to test positive for the remainder of the day but were clear of opiates after 18 hours. The likelihood of a false positive depends on the sensitivity of the drug test. In 1998, the cutoff level for opiate detection in the standard NIDA 5 test was raised from 300 ng/mL to 2,000 ng/mL to reduce the risk of false positives from poppy seed consumption. However, some toxicology labs still use the lower cutoff level, which increases the risk of false positives. Studies have shown that the morphine content of poppy seeds can vary significantly, with some batches containing as much as 251 µg/g. Depending on the potency of the seeds and the quantity consumed, it is possible to exceed the 2,000 ng/mL detection threshold. Due to the morphine content, the sale of poppy seeds from Papaver somniferum is banned in Singapore, and poppy seeds are also prohibited in Saudi Arabia for religious and drug control reasons. Culinary Uses Poppy seeds are widely used in the cuisines of Central and Eastern Europe. Sugared and ground poppy seeds are often combined with pasta or boiled with milk to create fillings or toppings for sweet pastries. In Bengali and Oriya cuisine, poppy seeds are also a common ingredient. In Mexico, the beer company Grupo Modelo, known for producing Corona beer, used red poppy flowers in its advertising until the 1960s. Poppies in Literature One of the most famous literary references to poppies appears in L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz and its 1939 film adaptation. In the novel, Dorothy and her companions encounter a field of poppies on their way to the Emerald City. The opium from the flowers causes Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion to fall asleep, while the Scarecrow and Tin Man, being non-living, are unaffected. They rescue Dorothy and enlist the help of the Queen of the Field Mice to transport the Lion out of the field. In the film adaptation, the poppy field is conjured by the Wicked Witch of the West and appears directly in front of the Emerald City. Dorothy and the Lion fall asleep, but Glinda intervenes by creating a snowfall that neutralizes the poppies' effects, allowing the group to continue their journey. Visual Depictions Poppies have been captured in various forms of art and photography, showcasing their beauty in gardens, fields, and natural landscapes. Examples include close-up images of Oriental poppies (Papaver orientale), fields of red corn poppies (Papaver rhoeas), and the golden California poppy (Eschscholzia californica). These images highlight the diverse forms and vibrant colors of poppies across different regions and settings.
